commentaries.description: कन्द के संपीड़न से शक्ति-चालन की इच्छा रखने वाले लेखक पहले कन्द के स्थान और स्वरूप को बताते हैं। यह गुदा के ऊपर और नाभि के नीचे स्थित है, जो पक्षी के अंडे के समान है। याज्ञवल्क्य कहते हैं कि यह गुदा से दो अंगुल ऊपर और मेढ़्र (लिंग) से दो अंगुल नीचे है, जो शरीर के मध्य में है। इसका विस्तार और आयाम चार अंगुल का है, जो त्वचा आदि से ढका हुआ, कोमल और धवल (सफेद) है। 'वितस्तिमात्रं' का अर्थ यहाँ कुल बारह अंगुल प्रमाण से है।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Suksma Sharira Anatomy (Kanda)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the precise anatomical location and dimensions of the Kanda, a vital nexus of the subtle energy body (nadi-chakra) situated near the pelvic region. It emphasizes that for the yogi, internal physiological mapping is essential for the effective practice of Shakti Chalana and Mudra.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It represents the traditional yogic concern with mapping the subtle internal body, which serves as a foundation for meditative concentration. In modern times, it highlights the bridge between somatic awareness and spiritual awakening.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practice includes the compression of the Kanda (Kandasampidana) to facilitate Shakti-chalana (arousing of energy).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Kanda acts as the 'mula' or root of all 72,000 nadis, acting as a crucial junction in the subtle anatomy (sukshma-sarira).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: It suggests that physiological landmarks serve as physical anchors for the mind to stabilize during meditation, facilitating the 'mind-body' connection.

sanskrit_shloka: सति वज्रासने पादौ कराभ्यां धारयेद् दृढम् ।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Hatha Yoga Posture Mechanics
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse focuses on the structural alignment of the body during seated meditative or yogic postures. By firmly holding the feet while in Vajrasana, the practitioner establishes a locked circuit of energy, stabilizing the spine and preparing the mind for internal withdrawal (pratyahara).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: These techniques are the historical precursors to modern somatic practices. In contemporary life, such 'locking' poses are used to alleviate back pain, improve digestive health through compression, and cultivate a sense of groundedness amidst high-stress environments.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practice includes the intentional tactile engagement of hands to feet, ensuring physical stability (Sthirata) as a prerequisite for subtle energy work.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of 'Vajrasana' (the Adamantine Pose) serves as the 'Sthira' (steadfast) foundation (Sthira-sukham) for Nadi-shodhana and Dhyana.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: From a psychological perspective, the act of holding the feet creates a 'closed-loop' bodily posture that signals safety and physiological containment to the autonomic nervous system, effectively reducing anxiety.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Kundalini Yoga / Hathayoga
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes a foundational state for the activation of internal spiritual energy. By anchoring the physical body in Vajrasana, the practitioner creates a stable conduit for the awakening and upward movement of the Kundalini Shakti.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes the body-mind connection, a principle prevalent in both ancient Vedic traditions and modern psychosomatic healing, where stability of form (asana) facilitates profound internal transformation.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The prescribed practice involves 'Vajrasana' (the thunderbolt posture) and the subtle physiological manipulation of the breath and internal energy ('cālayitvā') to stimulate the Kundalini.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept centers on 'Prana-sanchalana' (movement of life force) where the dormant potential energy known as 'Kundalini Shakti' is awakened from the 'Muladhara' through specific physical and energetic stabilization.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the mobilization of latent creative energy through focused discipline. Modern mindfulness and neuro-regulation practices often parallel these techniques, emphasizing the necessity of a stable physiological 'anchor' to process high-intensity mental or emotional experiences.

translation: One should perform the contraction (contraction or upward movement) of the sun (Surya/Prana), and thereafter stir (awaken) the Kundalini.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Hatha Yoga Physiology
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the subtle yogic process of redirecting Prana (the solar energy) to awaken the dormant spiritual power known as Kundalini. By controlling the 'sun' located in the navel region, the practitioner creates the necessary energetic pressure to stimulate Kundalini situated at the base of the spine.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: These practices form the core of Hatha Yoga traditions that bridge physical bodily control with elevated states of consciousness, emphasizing the interdependence of the human biological system and spiritual energy.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama, Uddiyana Bandha (implied), and Nadi-shodhana (energy circulation).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept involves Prana-samkoca (contraction of vital air) to facilitate Kundalini-jagarana (awakening of primordial energy) within the subtle anatomy (sukshma-sharira).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Modern neuro-somatic disciplines view this as 'vagal tone regulation' and deep diaphragmatic control to calm the nervous system and induce states of heightened mindfulness or flow.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Mudravidhanam (Practice of energetic seals)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse addresses the precise temporal discipline required in yogic practices, specifically within the context of Mudras. The practitioner is advised to maintain the rhythmic movement or state without the interference of psychological fear or doubt for a duration of two muhurtas.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It emphasizes the importance of 'Kala' (time) and 'Nirbhayata' (fearlessness) as prerequisites for attaining mastery in subtle physiological practices, common in Hatha Yoga traditions.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practice includes the sustained, rhythmic application of a specific Mudra or bodily movement for 96 minutes (two muhurtas) with a steady, undisturbed state of mind.
commentary_faqs.answer: The central concept is 'Abhyasa-Kala' (duration of practice) coupled with 'Nirbhayata', where fearlessness acts as a catalyst for the successful completion of the 'Cālanā' (movement of Prana).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this equates to 'flow state' or 'sustained focused attention.' It highlights that the efficacy of physical or meditative interventions depends on maintaining a calm, stress-free physiological state over a specific therapeutic window.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Kundalini Yoga and Nadi Shodhana
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse describes the essential mechanics of Yoga where the dormant primordial energy (Kundalini) is directed towards the entrance of the central energy channel, the Sushumna. This transition signifies the movement from mundane awareness to transcendental spiritual awakening.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In the modern era, this serves as a foundation for understanding psychophysiological integration, emphasizing the link between breath, energy, and mental focus.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama, Bandha (specifically Mula-bandha), and Nadi-shodhana are the implied practices to stimulate this movement.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept focuses on the 'mukhapravesha' or the entry of the 'Kundalini-shakti' into the 'Sushumna-nadi', which is the prerequisite for 'unmani-avastha'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the mobilization of subconscious potentials toward a centralized, focused, and integrated state of consciousness, alleviating inner fragmentation.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Kundalini Yoga / Shakti-chalan
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse refers to the activation of the subtle energy known as Kundalini, often allegorized as Arundhati. It emphasizes that constant practice is required to awaken this dormant spiritual potential residing within the human body.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This signifies the Hatha Yoga tradition's focus on physiological mastery to attain higher consciousness, which remains central to modern yoga practice and mindfulness.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Daily practice of Mudra-vidhana, focusing on deliberate energetic stimulation (sancalana) to disturb the static nature of the dormant Shakti.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Shakti-chalan' (stirring the Shakti), where the internal dormant energy is conceptualized as Arundhati, representing the latent spiritual potential (Kundalini) that must be awakened from its 'sukha-supta' (blissful rest) state to ascend the central channel.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the mobilization of subconscious resources and the regulation of the nervous system, translating the ancient yogic 'awakening' into modern terms of physiological resilience and self-actualization.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Shakti-patha / Kundalini Jagrana
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes that authentic yogic success is not theoretical but depends on the activation of inner energy (Shakti). Once the dormant power is set into motion, the practitioner transcends ordinary limitations and becomes a receptive vessel for spiritual attainments.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This reflects the Tantric and Hatha Yoga tradition where somatic practices are seen as the prerequisite for spiritual evolution, highlighting the importance of 'energy work' over mere intellectual study.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Mudrā-vidhāna, Prāṇāyāma, internal energy mobilization, and cultivation of steady meditative awareness.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of 'Śakti-sañcālana' involves the activation of the internal latent energy, distinguishing between mere physical exercise and the awakening of the Pranic force.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In a modern psychological context, this mirrors the process of self-actualization and the harnessing of one's dormant potential or 'flow states' to achieve peak performance and mental clarity.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (English)
commentaries.description: The Prana, being elongated by the breath flowing through the left and right nostrils (Ida and Pingala), becomes moon-like, filling the body with nectar before the 'striking of the bell' (the internal Anahata sound). After cutting through the time-bound fire (the consuming nature of temporal existence) and moving through the channel in the brow-aperture, the yogi renders the body anew, just like a tree whose trunk has been severed yet sprouts again.

After cutting through the time-bound fire (the consuming nature of temporal existence) and moving through the channel in the brow-aperture, the yogi renders the body anew, just like a tree whose trunk has been severed yet sprouts again.

commentaries.author: Jyotsnā (Hindi)
commentaries.description: इडा और पिंगला नाड़ियों से प्रवाहित वायु के कारण प्राण दीर्घ हो जाता है, और नाद (घंटिका) के प्रकटीकरण से पूर्व वह चंद्र के समान अमृत से शरीर को आप्लावित कर देता है। काल-अग्नि के वश को काटकर और भ्रूमध्य स्थित नाड़ी में गमन कर, योगी शरीर को पुनः नूतन कर लेता है, जैसे कटा हुआ वृक्ष पुनर्जीवित हो जाता है।

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Sattvic Discipline and Pranic Vitality
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse establishes the foundational lifestyle requirements for advanced yoga practice. Celibacy (Brahmacharya) preserves the subtle energy (Ojas), while dietary control (Hitamita) ensures internal purity, preventing the clogging of energy channels (Nadis).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In the modern era, this serves as a framework for 'energy management' and metabolic health. It emphasizes that mental and spiritual progress is inextricably linked to physiological equilibrium and the conservation of vital force.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Brahmacharya (conservation of energy), Mitahara (measured diet), and Nadi-krama (regulation of breath flow to achieve immortality/rejuvenation).
commentary_faqs.answer: The bhashya describes the transformation of Prana (Pranaparyaya) and the activation of the subtle body, specifically highlighting the role of Nadi-Shodhana and the eventual transcendence of Kala (Time) by accessing the Ajna Chakra (bhrūrandhra).

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the regulation of the autonomic nervous system. The 'rejuvenation' of the body corresponds to the reduction of cortisol and inflammatory markers, facilitating a state of deep, restorative neuro-biological health.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Kundalini Yoga and Pranayama
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse prescribes the awakening of the latent spiritual energy (Kundalini) followed by the 'Bhastra' or bellows breath, a type of intense pranayama. It emphasizes that physical breath control is a necessary tool to harness and direct the internal psychic energy.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This reflects the Hatha Yoga practice where the body is viewed as a laboratory. In modern contexts, it highlights the integration of respiratory control with neurological or energetic awareness.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribed practices include Kundalini-calana (stirring the energy) and Bhastra-kumbhaka (bellows-breath) to accelerate spiritual heat (tapas).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Kundalini-calana' or the stimulation of the dormant Shakti, which is essential to prepare the Nadi system for Pranic movement.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this equates to the regulation of the autonomic nervous system to achieve peak mental focus and energetic equilibrium, reducing lethargy and enhancing cognitive clarity.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Nadi Shodhana (Energetic Purification)
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse addresses the physiological and subtle anatomical framework of Yoga, where the human body is mapped as having 72,000 conduits (nadis) for prana. The purification of these channels is essential to remove blockages that hinder spiritual evolution and physical health.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This serves as the foundational justification for Pranayama and Kriya Yoga practices, emphasizing that internal cleanliness is a prerequisite for higher states of meditation and consciousness in Indian traditional health sciences.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama, Kumbhaka, Mudra-vidhana, and Sattvic lifestyle management.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of 'nadi-shodhana' pertains to the cleansing of the 'sūkṣma-śarīra' (subtle body). The 'mala' represents 'karmic' and 'tamasic' blockages within the 'prāṇavāha' system.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the clearing of neural and cognitive 'noise' or 'clutter.' In a modern context, it translates to the regulation of the autonomic nervous system to achieve homeostasis and stress reduction.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Hatha Yoga Physiology
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse highlights the Sushumna Nadi, the central energy channel in the subtle body. Through rigorous and consistent practice, the yogi activates this dormant channel, facilitating the upward movement of energy (Kundalini).

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This emphasizes the necessity of 'Abhyasa' (consistent practice) in spiritual life, paralleling modern psychological understanding of neuroplasticity and habit formation for mental transformation.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The prescribed practice is Dṛḍhābhyāsa, which denotes intense, steady, and unwavering commitment to yogic sadhana.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept focuses on Sushumna Nadi as the primary pathway of Pranic movement, distinguishing it from the dualistic Ida and Pingala channels.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept serves as a metaphor for focus and centration in a distracted world, where 'middle path' practice helps maintain physiological and psychological homeostasis.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Yoga-abhyasa and Chitta-vritti-nirodha
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes that the path to spiritual stillness requires the removal of lethargy and the disciplined focusing of the mind. Samadhi acts as the instrument through which the mind is anchored, preventing it from drifting into scattered states.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the necessity of 'vigilance' (apramada) in Indian meditative traditions, which remains a cornerstone for achieving success in any form of focused mental training, including modern mindfulness practices.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice involves 'Abhyasa' (consistent repetition), 'Vinidrata' (overcoming sleepiness/lethargy), and 'Dharana/Samadhi' (holding the mind firmly).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Yoga-nistha' achieved through the eradication of 'Tandra' (drowsiness) and the application of 'Samadhi' as the primary 'karana' (instrument) for 'Citta-ekagrata'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this addresses the need for 'sustained attention' and 'alertness' in an era of digital distraction, suggesting that meditative progress is impossible without first cultivating a wakeful and disciplined mental environment.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Necessity of Rajayoga in existence
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse posits that Rajayoga is the essential catalyst that gives meaning to worldly existence (Earth) and internal stillness (Night). Without the integration of the consciousness achieved through Rajayoga, both the material world and the repose of the night are devoid of spiritual purpose.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern times, it emphasizes that external success or physical rest is incomplete without the internal synchronization of the mind, bridging the gap between activity and conscious awareness.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Prescribes the internal mastery of the mind over mere physical 'asanas' or external rituals.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept addresses the 'vailakshanya' (distinction) of Rajayoga as the pinnacle of 'Mudravidhanam', rendering lower 'anga-s' ineffective if devoid of the 'dhyana' state.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this highlights the concept of 'mindfulness' vs 'mechanical habituation', suggesting that any action—no matter how 'grounded' (earth) or 'restful' (night)—lacks efficacy if performed with an un-integrated consciousness.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Pranayama and Chitta-Ekagrata
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse highlights the necessity of coupling physical breath control (Maruta-vidhi) with mental concentration (Manoyuktam). It asserts that the mechanics of yoga are ineffective if the consciousness is not actively tethered to the physiological process.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This underscores the classical yogic perspective that breath is the bridge between the body and mind, a concept foundational to modern mindfulness and breathing-based stress reduction techniques.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Pranayama, Dharana, Abhyasa (constant, focused repetition), Chitta-vritti-nirodha.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept revolves around 'Prana-samyamana' and the synchronization of 'Manas' with 'Vayu'. It emphasizes that external techniques ('Vidhi') must be internalised through 'Ekagrata' (one-pointed focus) to achieve the desired state of 'Yoga'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: In a modern psychological context, this relates to the 'mind-body connection' and the effectiveness of 'biofeedback'. It teaches that intentionality in breathing can regulate the nervous system, reduce anxiety, and improve cognitive performance by aligning physiological states with conscious attention.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Guruparampara and Yogic Authority
commentary_faqs.answer: This verse establishes the divine origin of the mudras, tracing them back to Adinatha (Shiva). It emphasizes that these practices are not merely human inventions but are revealed truths transmitted through the lineage of masters.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: It highlights the importance of traditional lineage (sampradaya) in validating spiritual practices. In the modern context, it suggests the necessity of authenticity and connection to a source of wisdom that transcends the individual ego.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The practice involves the systematic study and implementation of the ten specified mudras, recognized as foundational by the primary authority.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of 'Mudravidhanam' serves to formalize the practice of 'Mudras' as an authorized body of 'Sadhana' attributed to 'Adi-Natha', the original source of 'Yoga-Vidya'.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Modern relevance lies in the psychological grounding provided by authoritative frameworks, which prevent the dilution of wellness practices into superficial trends by grounding them in historical and philosophical depth.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Guru-Parampara and Authenticity
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse emphasizes that the knowledge of Mudras is not merely a technical skill, but a sacred transmission that must be inherited through a lineage. Authentic instruction (Sāmpradāyika) acts as the bridge between the practitioner and the divine efficacy of the gestures.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In the modern age of digital information, this verse reminds us of the necessity of 'lineage' and 'mentorship' over superficial learning, ensuring that esoteric practices remain rooted in experiential wisdom rather than mere theoretical curiosity.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Paramparā-upadeśa (lineage-based instruction) and Mudrā-abhyāsa (practice of mudras under guidance).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is Sāmpradāya-paramparā, the requirement that vidyā (knowledge) must be transmitted directly from a Guru who is established in the tradition to ensure spiritual validity.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: This addresses the psychological need for qualified mentorship; it highlights that complex internal techniques require a 'living' source to validate progress and prevent misapplication, shifting from information-gathering to transformative guidance.

commentary_faqs.answer: The verse highlights the necessity of absolute surrender to the instruction of the Guru as a prerequisite for success in technical yogic practices. Concentration (Samahita) is not merely physical focus but a deep mental absorption that aligns the student with the source of knowledge.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This emphasizes the lineage-based learning model (Guru-Shishya Parampara) still vital in modern yoga pedagogy, where the teacher's verbal guidance serves as the 'key' to unlock the physiological and subtle benefits of yogic mudras.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: Guru-upāsana (devotion to the teacher), Mudrā-abhyāsa (yogic gestural seals), and Samādhāna (mental equilibrium).
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept of Vakyaparatva signifies the internalization of the Guru's Vāk (logos/instruction), functioning as a catalyst for Samādhi within Mudrābhyāsa.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: This represents a psychological framework for mentorship where deep listening and cognitive alignment lead to the reduction of performance anxiety and improved mastery in any complex skill-based discipline.

commentary_faqs.question: Theme: Mudrā-vidhāna (The practice of mystical seals)
commentary_faqs.answer: Khechari represents the state of consciousness moving through the internal space of the cranial cavity (akasha). It bridges the individual life force with cosmic awareness by stabilizing the mind in the center of the void.

commentary_faqs.question: Cultural & Practical Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: In modern practice, it is understood as a technique of neuro-physiological regulation to achieve a state of deep meditative stillness and inner sensory withdrawal.

commentary_faqs.question: Yogic Practice: The prescribed practice involves physical and energetic locks (mudras) to control the flow of prana (vital force) toward the cranial center.
commentary_faqs.answer: The concept is 'Khechari' defined as the movement of consciousness (citta) in the void (kha) of the brahmarandhra, signifying the union of the practitioner with the cosmic space.

commentary_faqs.question: Modern Relevance & Therapeutic Benefit
commentary_faqs.answer: Psychologically, this represents the capacity to detach from external sensory stimuli (pratyahara) to achieve a state of equanimity and refined internal focus in an era of constant digital distraction.
